articles.title: AI bionic eye breakthrough could help restore sight
articles.summary: An AI bionic eye trained on a blind man's brain responses helped UC Santa Barbara researchers produce more predictable phosphenes with less current.
articles.body: At a hospital in Spain, a 27-year-old man who lost his sight after a traumatic brain injury reported seeing flashes of light when researchers stimulated part of his brain. Those flashes were limited, but scientists have now used artificial intelligence to gain more control over the brain activity behind them. The research could help make future artificial vision systems more reliable. Scientists are developing an AI bionic eye approach that learns how an individual's brain responds to electrical stimulation. Although the technology remains experimental, it could eventually help people who have lost their sight regain some degree of vision. So, how does this brain implant work, and what would it take to turn a few flashes of light into useful vision? MOUTHPAD LETS YOUR TONGUE CONTROL A COMPUTER Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. How an AI bionic eye works When you look at something, your eyes send signals to your brain, which processes what you're seeing. But what happens when those signals can no longer reach the brain? For years, scientists have been developing electronic implants that attempt to restore some vision. Some stimulate the retina, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye. Others take a different approach by sending electrical signals directly to the brain. That's what makes this research interesting. Scientists are studying a device called a visual cortical prosthesis, sometimes described as a bionic eye. Despite the nickname, the implant goes into the brain rather than the eye. It targets the visual cortex, the part of the brain responsible for processing visual information. When researchers stimulate this area with electricity, a person may experience flashes or spots of light known as phosphenes. These sensations can resemble glowing dots or simple shapes. However, getting the brain to produce consistent results has been a major challenge. A blind man helps researchers test the brain implant In 2024, researchers from UC Santa Barbara traveled to Spain as part of a collaborative study with ETH Zurich and Miguel Hernández University involving a 27-year-old man who had lost his sight after a traumatic brain injury. At IMED Elche Hospital, the man had received an experimental implant containing 96 electrodes placed in his visual cortex. The device was intended to remain implanted for six months before being removed. During the study, researchers delivered small electrical currents through the electrodes. The man reported experiencing flashes of light and various shapes. That was encouraging, but the researchers wanted to go further. They needed to understand why certain electrical signals produced particular sensations and whether those responses could become more predictable. FIRST-EVER GENE THERAPY FOR HEARING LOSS GETS FDA APPROVAL: 'GROUNDBREAKING' How AI makes the bionic eye more precise This is where artificial intelligence helped the researchers make progress. Scientists trained a deep learning model to study how the man's brain responded to different electrical stimulation patterns. Instead of relying solely on the settings sent to the electrodes, the AI analyzed the actual brain activity those signals produced. It also considered what the brain was doing immediately before stimulation. That's important because brain activity can fluctuate over time, which can affect how someone responds to the same electrical signals. Using this information, researchers identified stimulation patterns more likely to produce particular brain responses. When they tested those AI-designed patterns, the results improved. The researchers achieved greater accuracy in producing their intended patterns of brain activity while using less electrical current. They also discovered something important. The brain activity recorded after stimulation was a better predictor of what the man reported seeing than the electrical settings alone. In other words, knowing how the brain responded gave researchers a better indication of the man's visual experience. Michael Beyeler, an associate professor at UC Santa Barbara who helped lead the research, explained the goal. "Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around," he said. That approach could help future implants adjust to changes in brain activity rather than depend on the same stimulation settings every time. The research was published in the journal Neuron. Could an AI bionic eye restore actual vision? It's an exciting possibility, but there's still a long road ahead. The man in this experiment experienced flashes and shapes of light. He did not regain normal eyesight, and researchers have yet to demonstrate that this AI approach can provide the functional vision someone would need to read or recognize faces. The experiment also involved only one participant. Scientists need additional research to determine how well the approach works in other people. Still, the findings address a significant challenge. Researchers can stimulate the brain, but predicting exactly what someone will experience has been difficult. AI could help close that gap by learning how each person's brain responds and identifying better ways to deliver electrical signals. We've also covered a tiny retinal implant that helped people with advanced age-related macular degeneration regain some central vision. That device works with the retina and specialized glasses. The new research takes a different route by targeting the brain directly. It could eventually offer another option for people whose eyes or optic nerves can no longer send visual information effectively, provided their visual cortex can still respond to stimulation. ROBOT PERFORMS 26 CATARACT SURGERIES WITH SURGEON CONTROL What needs to happen before bionic eyes become available? Researchers still have several challenges to overcome before this technology could become a practical treatment. First, they need to demonstrate that the approach works safely and consistently in more people. Scientists must also determine whether the flashes and shapes produced by electrical stimulation can become useful visual information. Another challenge involves keeping the implant responsive as the brain changes. A stimulation pattern that works during one session may produce different results later. The AI approach tested in this study offers a possible way to address that problem. However, researchers have yet to demonstrate a complete system that continuously adapts and delivers useful vision during everyday activities. For people dealing with vision loss today, technology already provides other forms of assistance. Our article on tech tools that make vision loss easier to manage at CyberGuy.com explores features that can help with everyday tasks. As for this new research, the next challenge involves turning more predictable brain responses into visual experiences that could help someone navigate the world. Kurt's key takeaways The possibility of helping someone regain their sight through a brain implant is pretty remarkable. What I find especially interesting about this research is how AI could help scientists understand the way each person's brain responds to electrical signals. That could eventually make artificial vision more reliable. But there's still a big difference between seeing flashes of light and being able to recognize what's around you. I'd love to see this technology reach a point where someone who has lost their sight can recognize familiar objects or move around more independently. We're not there yet, and this was only one participant. Still, if researchers can turn these early results into useful vision, it could make an enormous difference in people's lives. If scientists could someday restore even a small amount of your vision through a brain implant, would you consider the surgery, or would you wait until the technology could provide clearer sight? articles.title: Israel kills four in Gaza as Hamas chief al-Hayya’s son survives strike
articles.summary: Four of Khalil al-Hayya’s other sons were previously killed by Israeli forces, according to the Palestinian group.
articles.body:
A son of Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya has survived an Israeli air strike targeting his family in Gaza, said the Palestinian group.

The air raid on Friday came as Israeli attacks elsewhere in the strip killed four Palestinians, despite the so-called “ceasefire” agreed over a year ago.

Izzeldeen al-Hayya, 29, and his family survived the Israeli strike at dawn, said Hamas official Basem Naim. Hamas sources told the Reuters news agency that several relatives were wounded, including the daughter-in-law of the Hamas chief.

The family of another of Khalil al-Hayya’s deceased sons, Azzam, also survived.

Naim described Izzeldeen as the Hamas leader’s last surviving son. Four of his brothers were killed by Israeli forces: Hamza in 2008, Osama in 2014, Humam in September last year and Azzam in May this year.

Izzeldeen is the twin brother of Humam, who was killed in an Israeli strike on Hamas leaders in Qatar last year. Khalil al-Hayya narrowly escaped that attack during negotiations. He was named leader of Hamas in July.

Hamas condemned Friday’s attack, describing it as an attempt to “assassinate” al-Hayya’s son and target his family.

The group linked the attack to threats made against its leader by Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz and accused Israel of seeking to undermine the October 2025 “ceasefire” agreement. Hamas said the “cowardly act” exposes the “complete detachment from human and moral values” of Israeli leaders.

Deadly Israeli attacks continued elsewhere in Gaza on Friday.

A Palestinian was killed and several others wounded in a drone att on a vehicle in northern Gaza, according to the Palestinian Wafa news agency.

Wafa named the victim as Khaled Assaf and quoted witnesses as saying a vehicle was struck in the Bir al-Naaja area, west of the Jabalia refugee camp.

In the southern city of Rafah, Civil Defence teams recovered the bodies of three Palestinians and rescued two wounded people following an attack near Muawiya Mosque on al-Bahr Street, Wafa reported.

Israeli army gunfire injured a Palestinian child in the al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis in southern Gaza.

Medical sources and witnesses told Wafa that Israeli forces repeatedly opened fire on tents sheltering displaced people in the area from their positions near the eastern “Yellow Line”.

Friday’s attacks followed a series of Israeli raids on Thursday that killed 10 Palestinians, including a senior education official.

Also on Friday, Hamas described as “ridiculous” the Israeli army’s claim that it used one of the buildings at Al-Ahli Baptist Hospital in Gaza City as an interrogation centre.

The Israeli military and Shin Bet made the allegations on Thursday, claiming Hamas was conducting military activities within the hospital complex.

The Israeli claim “comes as part of the ongoing incitement against hospitals in the Gaza Strip”, Hamas said in a statement.

Hospitals are “public places open to all civil and UN institutions operating in the enclave”, it noted, adding that Israel had never provided evidence to substantiate any of its claims.

The Episcopal Diocese of Jerusalem, which oversees the hospital, said it had no knowledge of any secret interrogation centre on the premises.

According to Gaza’s Health Ministry, Israeli violations of the October 2025 “ceasefire” since it took effect have killed at least 1,705 Palestinians and wounded 6,163. Israel has killed at least 74,772 Palestinians in Gaza since the genocidal war began in October 2023.

articles.title: Low levels of common vitamin could be stealing nearly 30 minutes of your sleep
articles.summary: Low vitamin D blood levels were linked to about 23 minutes less sleep per night in a new study of adults 40 and older that used wearable sensors.
articles.body: Middle-aged and older adults with low levels of vitamin D slept about 23 minutes less per night than people with normal levels, according to a new study that tracked sleep with wearable sensors. The study, led by the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health and the National Institute on Aging, used data collected from 2012 to 2019 as part of the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging. The researchers looked at blood tests and sleep data from 460 adults ages 40 and older, averaging 71 years of age. ONE TYPE OF SLEEP LINKED TO DRAMATICALLY LOWER RISK OF DEMENTIA, PARKINSON'S AND 81 OTHER DISEASES After dividing the participants into three groups by vitamin D level, they found that the highest group slept nearly 20 minutes longer each night than the group with the lowest levels. People with lower levels also stayed awake longer after waking up at night — a pattern that held regardless of age, gender or race. The connection between vitamin D and sleep was strongest among Black participants, who made up about 22% of the group. "Black adults in the United States have a higher prevalence of vitamin D deficiency and sleep disturbances compared to White adults, and may benefit more from increasing vitamin D levels," lead author Diefei Chen, a doctoral candidate in epidemiology at the Bloomberg School, said in a press release. CAN WEARABLES DETECT HEART PROBLEMS EARLY? DOCTOR BREAKS DOWN REAL DATA Most earlier studies on vitamin D and sleep relied on people reporting how well they thought they slept. In this study, researchers used blood draws and actigraphs, which are watch-like motion sensors that measure sleep and wake times. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The team also checked vitamin B12, which previous studies linked to sleep. While higher levels correlated with less nighttime wakefulness in women and more in men, the authors noted the results were statistically inconclusive. The findings were published on Oct. 14 in The Journal of Gerontology: Medical Sciences. Poor sleep and vitamin D deficiency are both widespread among older adults, with previous research linking sleep disturbances to higher risks of dementia, heart disease and diabetes. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES The study had several limitations. Because the researchers looked at snapshots of data rather than testing a treatment in a clinical trial, they could only establish a link between vitamin D and sleep. The findings did not prove that low levels cause poor sleep or that taking supplements will fix it. Because blood tests can't distinguish between vitamin D from sunlight, food or supplements, the study could not determine whether the source matters. In addition, the researchers did not track whether changing a person's vitamin D levels over several years leads to changes in their sleep. articles.title: Kate Middleton Details Being in the Hospital for Cancer Treatment in New Doc: ‘A Really Dark Time’
articles.summary: Catherine, Princess of Wales, is revealing she endured “scary” and “dark” moments during her cancer treatment. The former Kate Middleton has a new documentary.
articles.body: Catherine, Princess of Wales, is revealing she endured “scary” and “dark” moments during her cancer treatment, and the simple gesture that made her feel better, in her new documentary. The British royal announced her diagnosis in 2024, without publicly sharing the type of cancer she was dealing with. The following year, she said she completed treatment and is now in remission. In “Heal: A Princess of Wales Special,” the former Kate Middleton describes what it was like to be in a hospital and the comfort of having someone there to support her. “When you’re on your hospital bed and it is so clinical around you — you haven’t got fresh air, no greenery around you. It’s very stark and alien and stripped back. The darkness was a really scary, disorientating experience. I think I was sort of in and out of consciousness. It was a really dark time,” she says in the documentary. “But also then somewhere through that, too, when I became aware of someone holding my hand. They weren’t talking to me. They weren’t trying to fix anything. They were just there, and the presence of someone that stood by me in that time, I’ll forever be grateful for. “It really made me realize the importance of simply being alongside somebody through their darkest times. So often you think you need to fix something or say something or do something, and you don’t. You just need to be there, and that’s what love looks like. That’s what I think the light is that we can often find out of the darkest of times.” “Heal” premieres on NBC on Nov. 30 at 8 p.m. ET/PT. The documentary airs on Bravo at 11:30 p.m. ET/PT the same day and streams the following day on Peacock. It’s a “deeply personal look” at the royal’s life after her cancer diagnosis and remission, according to a news release from NBCUniversal, the parent company of NBC, TODAY and Peacock. TODAY former co-anchor Hoda Kotb, who is a breast cancer survivor, will give a special introduction. The film includes footage of the princess and her younger brother, James, hiking the National Three Peaks Challenge in the UK, which involves summiting the three highest peaks of Scotland, England and Wales within 24 hours.

articles.title: Kate Middleton Tearfully Shares How Her Kids Motivated Her During Cancer Recovery in New Doc
articles.summary: In a new documentary, Kate Middleton shares that her three children were her motivation to complete cancer treatment and recover and how they keep inspiring hertoday.
articles.body: Catherine, Princess of Wales, is opening up about her struggles during cancer treatment and what kept her motivated like never before in a new documentary, “Heal.” The former Kate Middleton, 44, revealed how her children played a crucial role in her recovery. She and her husband, Prince William, share two sons and a daughter: Prince George, 13, Princess Charlotte, 11, and Prince Louis, 8. In the documentary, the mother of three gets deeply personal about her experience being diagnosed with cancer at 42 and finding strength in the face of serious illness. Reflecting on her treatments and recovery, Kate described moments of “darkness” and facing her “own mortality.” The royal said she credits her children for motivating her to keep going and get better. “They gave me the reason to get out of hospital,” Kate said, fighting back tears. Kate first revealed she was diagnosed with cancer in March 2024 following an abdominal surgery that January. In a statement, she shared that she was receiving preventative chemotherapy and being treated at the Royal Marsden Hospital in London. The Princess of Wales has never publicly disclosed which type of cancer she had. In September 2024, Kate revealed she had finished chemo. She has been in remission for nearly two years, since January 2025. In “Heal,” she reflects on her cancer journey while conquering the National Three Peaks Challenge, with her brother, James Middleton. The hike, which is one of the toughest endurance challenges in the United Kingdom, involves climbing three of the tallest peaks in England, Scotland and Wales in 24 hours. Again, Kate credits her three children for getting her through. “They gave me the reason to finish this challenge and get home,” Kate told James in the documentary. In an emotional moment at the second peak’s summit, James plays Kate recorded voice messages from each of her children: “Hello, mommy. I really love you, and I hope you do well going up the mountain. Remember, I’m always in your heart with you, and I love you very much,” Louis said. “We’re all thinking of you right now. ... You look really really strong. Keep going, and we’re right behind you. Love you so much. See you when you get back,” George added. “Mommy. I love you so much. We are so proud of you doing your walk and your challenges. We really wish you good luck, and I’ll be cheering you on,” said Charlotte. Her children also greeted her when she finished the challenge, another emotional moment captured in the documentary. “Heal” airs on NBC on Nov. 30 at 8 p.m. ET and streams on Peacock Dec. 1. All proceeds go to cancer research and treatment.

articles.title: 3 sanitary workers suffocate to death in Maharashtra's Sangli septic tank; negligence, say cops
articles.summary: KOLHAPUR: Three conservancy workers suffocated to death within 15 minutes of entering a septic tank at Shirdhon village in Sangli’s Kavathe Mahankal
articles.body: KOLHAPUR: Three conservancy workers suffocated to death within 15 minutes of entering a septic tank at Shirdhon village in Sangli’s Kavathe Mahankal taluka on Friday, police said.The owner of a private hotel and lawn along Pandharpur road had hired the workers to clean the tank. Five workers arrived in the morning to carry out the task. Yashwant Biru Shelake (50) entered the tank first. When he did not respond to calls, Akash Anil Bagade (23) went down to rescue him, police said. After neither responded, Tushar Balasaheb Koshti (25) entered the tank.All three were brought out and taken to Kavathe Mahankal’s sub-district hospital, where doctors declared them dead on arrival, police said.“Preliminary investigation indicated negligence in the septic tank deaths.
